# Introduction

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

import seaborn as sns

sns.set_context('talk')

df = sns.load_dataset('flights')
```
RQ: Do the number of flights increase over the years?

An advid traveler is looking to become a history buff and see if there is any relationship to the 
amount of flights over the years. They plan to look at the seaborn dataset flights that has a total
of `{python} f"{df.shape[0]}"` trips.


# Literature Review


# Methods

Given that we have two coloumns of continuous data (year and passenger)
 we will evalute this relationship using simple correlation analysis and also a scatter plot.
These two methods are classic and tradtional starting points when evaluting data like these.

# Results

```{python}
corr_val = df['year'].corr(df['passengers'])

narative = "a very strong negative correaltion"

if corr_val > 0.8: 
    narrative = "a very strong positive correlation"
elif corr_val > .4:
    narrative = "a moderate postive correaltion"
elif corr_val > 0:
    narrative = "a positve but weak correlation"
elif corr_val > -.4:
    narrative = "a moderate negative correaltion"
```
Using the classic simple Pearson correlation approach these data produce a correltation coefficent of
`{python} f"{corr_val}"`, as such, given this result, we conclude that the relationship is `{python} f"{narrative}"`.

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

#| label: fig-length-width-scatter
#| fig-cap: "A scatterplot of petal length and petal width"

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))

sns.scatterplot(data = df, y = 'passengers', x = 'year')

plt.ylabel('passengers')
plt.xlabel('years')
```

As shown in @fig-length-width-scatter we set additional evidence of a strong positive correlation
between an iris flower petal length and petal width
